lesson.title: The Mental Encyclopedia: Semantic Memory
lesson.summary: Semantic memory is the explicit memory system that stores general knowledge and facts about the world, independent of when or where that knowledge was learned.
lesson.body:
Semantic memory is the part of explicit memory that stores general knowledge and facts about the world, independent of any particular time or place a person learned them. Knowing that a triangle has three sides, that ice is frozen water, or that Paris is the capital of France are all semantic memories. Psychologist Endel Tulving originally proposed dividing explicit, or declarative, memory into two systems: semantic memory for general facts and concepts, and episodic memory for personally experienced events tied to a specific time and place. Semantic memory is what remains once the personal context of learning has faded away and only the fact itself endures.

Semantic memory belongs to the explicit memory system because retrieving it, at least when done deliberately, involves a conscious sense of knowing. Answering a trivia question or defining a word requires actively and consciously bringing information to mind, which is exactly what separates explicit memory from implicit memory, where past experience shapes behavior without any accompanying awareness of remembering. What makes semantic memory a distinctive kind of explicit memory is that this conscious retrieval usually comes stripped of any memory for the original learning episode. Most people know that Paris is the capital of France without recalling the specific classroom, book, or conversation where they first learned it.

Semantic memory is generally thought to be organized as a network of interconnected concepts rather than as an unstructured list of isolated facts. Closely related concepts are linked together, so that activating one concept makes closely related concepts easier and faster to retrieve, a pattern known as semantic priming. Hearing the word "nurse," for example, tends to speed up recognition of the related word "doctor" more than it speeds up recognition of an unrelated word like "bread," because "nurse" and "doctor" sit close together within the same associative network. This networked structure is part of why semantic memory supports fast, flexible reasoning: activating one idea automatically brings related ideas within easy reach.

Semantic memory accumulates gradually over a lifetime, built up through repeated exposure, teaching, reading, and experience that gets generalized into stable facts and concepts. A young child slowly builds a semantic memory network of categories like "animal," "food," and "furniture" through countless individual encounters with specific instances of each. Over time the specific instances fade from memory while the general pattern they taught the child remains, which is precisely why semantic memory can feel disconnected from any particular episode even though episodic experiences are what built it in the first place.

Because semantic and episodic memory are both explicit systems, they are closely related, but they are not identical, and certain forms of brain damage can affect one while relatively sparing the other. In semantic dementia, a progressive neurological condition, patients gradually lose general factual knowledge, forgetting what common objects and words mean, while their memory for specific recent personal events can remain comparatively intact for a longer time. Cases like this suggest that semantic and episodic memory, while both explicit, rely on at least partially separate neural resources within the brain's broader explicit memory system.
